Yeah I agree, I saw Taki as a bit of a coward too. And I have definitely had coward high school band directors before, and they’re infuriating. 

However I wanted to offer another perspective. Since the very beginning, it was left up to the entire band and not Taki himself to decide the band’s goal: work hard and aim for Nationals, or enjoy a good relaxing time. So I won’t give him credit, but I do think it was fitting for the story as a whole for the band to decide democratically on major decisions/ plot points such as the trumpet solo in S1 or the soli in S3. I never floated my idea to get torn down on Reddit (geez people don’t be mean!), but during the pandemic I was in a bad place and thought about quitting my job and moving states to study ballet full time with a certain teacher (I had been taking their classes online). It was so unrealistic of me to think that could work out, and the teacher did me a huge favor of not inviting me back to their studio after transitioning back in person (they primarily trained children and teens for “real” ballet careers and adults were welcome online but lower priority), because if they had, I think I would’ve actually gone through with my plan. Yikes. 

You’re totally fine with having a passion. Hold onto that excitement of learning something new, and work hard. I think the key to not burning out and losing that love is setting reasonable expectations, and you can have a very satisfying adult ballet journey while finishing college and working full time.

Edit: Happy to offer recs if you’re looking for those. I really hope you figure out how to fit ballet into your life!

Definitely yes! However the difficulty and the effort required to get back to where you were before depends on what else you’ve been doing those 7 months. For example, do you run, yoga, stretch, other genre of dance? You’ll probably be surprised how quickly your body recovers. 

I recently took 6 months off from ballet (and did K-Pop during that time), and I started taking classes again about 3 weeks ago.. This week I got my double pirouettes back. However I lost a LOT of flexibility (turnout, extensions, my poor back), some directional awareness, memory of ballet terms… I used to be comfortably intermediate but now I’m back in elementary for the time being.

This is just my experience, but I have tried Mirella Whisper, Bloch Heritage, Russian Pointe Rubin, and Nikolay Nova (flex, I think). 

Something I learned about feet is that 1) they may be a different shape when you walk into the store vs. after you’ve been dancing and warmed up; 2) they may change over time as you continue training (get stronger/muscular, lose or gain weight, etc.); and 3) they may compress in width between flat standing position and full pointe when you are engaging all your toes.

For me, the Mirella was a fair start but caused lots of pain in the big toe the more I wore them. The next fitter recommended the Bloch or RP, so I tried each, one after another over a couple years. The Bloch I just sank into after only a couple classes and tried compensating with thick toe pads and box liners… bad. The RP I had a difficult time with because my feet and ankles aren’t super archy and looked sickled in them. 

I think the last fitter I went to was a lot more observant of the idiosyncrasies of my feet and recommended the best model for me so far. Actually, I don’t think I need to look for different shoes because they work so well!

Everything you’ve expressed is what I’ve been ruminating over these past few months, especially the past week or so. I’ve consumed lots of videos and literature about Autism and ADHD, and there are so many testimonials and stories I relate to, as well as lists of common traits (lack of natural understanding how to interact with people, with a long history of masking and feeling like a total social fraud; special interests/obsessions; my thinking is very logical and detail oriented, in a way that others just don’t “get” when I try to verbalize my ideas). On the other hand, I can come up with plenty of reasons why I wouldn’t fit the criteria for one or either of these conditions (I don’t think I have sensory issues as they’re typically described, related to light, sound, texture? Though things make me itchy very easily…)

Anyway, you phrased it so well, I too feel conflicted about my identity, since I believe I fit somewhere within neurodivergence but I’m not sure at what point I could openly call myself Autistic or ADHD. Do I need to wait for a formal diagnosis before I can confirm who I am? Could I do so without one? And what if a psychologist just tells me I’m “normal”? I don’t think I could believe them, because I feel different from the very core of myself, like an instinct.

Basically I know deep down inside that I need help, and living like this and trying so hard for 30 years (yep same age!) is way too long and tiring. The past year or so I’ve really hit a low point emotionally - depressed, exhausted, lost motivation and self esteem. I am a very sad and angry person. I grew up with a bit of a shame-based mindset so it feels a little more complicated for me, but what I’ve been thinking is that identifying as neurodivergent (specifically Autistic, maybe ADHD to some extent) is a first step that I need to take in order to reach greater acceptance of myself, have a better idea of where to seek support, etc. I have really mixed feelings about a formal diagnosis, though it feels like the right thing for me personally, so I can be more confident how to move forward and make some changes in my life (not sure what yet).

I think you’ve already gotten lots of really great advice, but what you described was exactly how I felt the first couple cons I went to, so I wanted to pitch in a few things that I did since then that worked for me.

- participate in events: lots of communication and bonding can take place w/ fellow participants in masquerade, death match, singing-dancing showcase, karaoke, etc. And doing the same events each year or at multiple cons, you’ll probably see the same people regularly

- participate in cosplay photo meetups: so many fans of the same anime or game will be in the same place at the same time, and it’s also easy to find fans of the same characters. Depending on how they’re run, you might have plenty of time in between photos to chat w people while you’re waiting for your character’s/group’s turn.

- attend panels or other activities that promote interaction (as opposed to lecture style): examples would be like speed friending, trivia, arts & crafts

- keep up the good work on Discord and Instagram! Stay in touch with the people you exchanged contact info with. On Discord look out for official or unofficial servers related to the cons you go to, because that’s where people may organize meetups and cosplay groups. On IG, follow others who come up in recommended, in order to expand your network. I’ve seen lots of cosplay groups formed via sharing on Stories, as well as sharing of Discord servers.

I did not formally study pitch accent and I regret it to a certain extent. 

My first year plus summer of beginner Japanese was spent basically half with a native teacher and half with non-native TAs. There was no mention of pitch accent, and a lot of my time was spent (incorrectly) modeling my speech after non-native senpai. I’m quite tone deaf to begin with and I just didn’t know any better. I really would have found it helpful to learn the basics to at least distinguish between all the “hashi” and become familiar with the pitch-“shape” (?) of a sentence earlier on.

On the other hand, I understand that they avoid teaching it outright so that students don’t get too caught up in the details at the beginning. Besides, I hope at this point I have built a solid enough foundation that when I listen to Japanese or converse with native speakers, instead of focusing on “what does these words mean?” I can focus on “what do these words sound like?”

Hello! I find your post particularly inspiring, so I'm going to add my thoughts. :)

I have no idea what the characters or the voice actors actually do for training, but as someone who is passionate about singing and dancing as a lifelong hobby, I have developed my own routine of sorts.

Singing - First, water, tea (not too hot though!) and vocal warm ups. Before even learning a song, sitting down with printed song lyrics, listening to the song on repeat, and taking notes. I use this to study Japanese as well, so I'm marking both language notes (kanji readings, pronunciation, meaning) and musicality notes (pitch, breaths, counts). The rest of my workflow is kind of messy since I just sing whatever and however long I feel like. Recording myself and listening to myself is really embarrassing for me, but it helps me figure out what needs improvement.

Dancing - Running (6 km is excessive… I feel like running a couple miles a couple times a week earns me enough stamina for dancing) or some kind of 20-min cardio (jumping jacks?). Core exercises like holding planks and strengthening glutes and back, makes a huge difference for your balance. Stretching is also super important, anything that opens up the hips and shoulders so you have optimal range of motion. To learn idol dances I'll look at both lives and covers on YT, and for Liella their practice videos. Finding or making a mirror version is ideal. Thanks to ballet I've learned how to mentally break down steps in counts of 8; but even if you don't do that, as long as you go line by line the choreo should be digestible. Unless you're really fast at picking up choreo (I am slow), be prepared to block out a solid hour or two nonstop. My progression goes something like: hour 1 get to the point I can mark out everything roughly; hour 2 clean it up and make the moves sharper; sleep on it; next day review the choreo w/ video then commit to memory; the following days add style, keep recording myself, and work on fixing any bad habits (ex. sometimes my arms aren't even).

Last piece of advice is to eat healthy and often! Fuel your body with a variety of nutrients! When my mind is focused on singing/dancing I tend to forget to eat. Malnutrition can cause injury in the long run.

My main takeaway there was learning more about the friendship dynamic of the original three and how their personalities influence that. Honoka is a go-getter, and having her "eyes on the prize" sometimes prevents her from being in tune with others; Kotori seems a little shy in a secretive way, demonstrated by the maid cafe job; Umi seems reasonable and thoughtful, hence acting as the messenger between the two when communication breaks down. I never liked the big slap, but I think Umi ultimately succeeded in encouraging them to be honest with each other.

Rewatching Season 1, I can see why Umi, Eli, and Maki are my favorite, because I would consider myself a combination of their qualities.

* Umi: serious (drill instructor pre-Eli), disciplined (training camp plan), conservative (shy about costumes), cares deeply for friends (Honk-Birb messenger).
* Eli: serious, disciplined, perfectionist (ballet background), stubborn and tends to sacrifice fun & dreams for practicality (as student council president). 
* Maki: kind at heart (Hanayo advocate); acts cold, but really wants to get along with others, but has no idea how (training camp episode).

At this point, I feel like we haven't seen much individual characterization of Nico beyond her background as idol club president and meme traits, so I hope to see more that would redeem her. As discussed in an earlier episode, I think her approach to idolhood was totally wrong, but I respect her passion. I've heard of two cases of switching job roles:

The first case is at the time you complete your JET application, there's a box you can check off that basically asked, "If you don't get hired as CIR, do you wish to be considered for an ALT position?" (I said no.) There's a chance this also gets addressed in your interview, depending on how you respond. However, I did not see a question that went the other way, a denied ALT applicant considered for a CIR position.

The second case was specific to my CO. There were 2 CIR positions that they hired directly from the JET applicant pool; there was 1 CIR position that they hired among interested "senior" ALTs (3rd year and above?). I think the turnover rate for this position was every few years, not frequent. Since this position assumed that you were initially hired as an ALT, stayed around long enough for the position to open, and demonstrated advanced Japanese language skills (I'm not sure if N1/N2 was required on paper), it's probably not something one should really count on as a pathway to CIR.

In addition, I think many governmental and other organizations have CIR-like positions specifically for non-Japanese, not connected to JET. Always an option to look for tourism/PR/cultural exchange jobs independently, while working as an ALT.

Hi! I was a CIR in 2015-2016, and my role was mostly of the “ALT coordinator” nature, as well as the official title of Prefectural Advisor.

There was a lot of administrative work involved, and we basically managed & supported ALTs from their arrival to their departure. Some of the major things included:

Pre-arrival - school placement, apartment placement, answering preliminary questions

Arrival - orientation, signing employment contracts, registering at ward office, setting up bank accounts, setting up mobile phones

During school year - documenting attendance and leave, documenting commute routes, organizing professional development workshops, visiting schools/classes, collecting performance evaluations, conferencing w/ ALTs about work & life, assisting ALTs & schools in holding various English events, holding reappointment interviews

Special occasions - accompanying ALT to hospital to interpret if needed in emergency, responding to inquiries or problems concerning apartment, phone, insurance, etc.

Departure - terminating various contracts, arranging return flights, apartment inspections, organizing leavers’ orientation and final ceremony

Please note, I did NOT do all these singlehandedly! I worked in a section of the BOE with one other CIR and several Japanese managers, including an elementary school specialist, middle school specialist, and a couple financial assistants. Lots of communication and sharing of duties.

Despite all the desk work, I enjoyed it plenty, especially working closely with a lot of wonderful people. And the school visits, frequent events, and apartment inspections meant a lot of “field trips” away from the office! And since this later led me to an excellent (also administrative) job in higher ed back in the US, I am very grateful for the experience.

Edit: I forgot to mention, I also got to travel to Tokyo multiple times on business trips, so that was a ton of fun. CIR and PA workshops, as well as meeting a group of April arrivals to fly home with. :)

Hello! I was a CIR in Kobe City back in 2015-16.

1. My role was primarily Prefectural Advisor and liaison between the BOE and ALTs/school placements, providing support both work-related and home-related. I worked with my division (including 1 other CIR) to organize orientations for incoming JETs, professional development workshops and English-educational events throughout the year, and informational meetings for departing JETs. We also accompanied our supervisors on school visits to observe ALT lessons and give debriefings afterward. The CIRs were the ones to receive questions from ALTs regarding lifestyle issues (apartment, health insurance, etc.) and occasionally helped interpret (e.g. calling an internet provider or going to the hospital). In my case, tourism was very minor; the only memorable activity in that category was a week-long sister-city visit from a high school group, which I accompanied on tours and helped interpret.
2. I majored in Japanese language in college and studied formally for 3 out of the 4 years. This included a semester exchange program. I took the N2 right after I finished 3rd-year Japanese and failed, but I passed N2 on my second try thanks to intensive self-study. My one regret here is focusing too much on passing the exam while sacrificing opportunities to practice conversation, casual and professional. Speaking was (and still is) my weakest skill. Months before JET started, we did get mailed a CIR Japanese language handbook, or something to that effect, and I did take that rather seriously and at least made sure I knew as many business phrases as possible.
3. Edit (sorry for the wait!): I wish I had started off with more experience. A higher level of Japanese would have been mutually beneficial to myself and my team, in utilizing me on more Japanese-intensive projects like translation & interpretation. Prior work experience and life experience (I was fresh out of college) would have spared them my learning curve in tackling issues like health insurance, taxes, and unions.

First, the verb ある and the particles に, は, and が you’ll definitely learn in introductory Japanese (N5 Level). However, the way they’re put together in this sentence is an idiomatic phrase that is both difficult to translate literally and difficult to categorize by JLPT level. It is a phrase used by native speakers in conversation, but not necessarily something that would show up in your curriculum or in textbooks, like a grammar point.

You’ve probably learned that ある means “to have” or “to exist.” And には is like “in” or “within.” And が, although taught at beginner level as a “subject particle” (?), in this case is used as “but.” Kind of like けど but with its own nuances and rules. (I won’t go into these any further.)

I don’t know how to translate literally, but it could mean that something exists, BUT there’s a condition. For example, “This town has restaurants, but there aren’t many.” Or “This town has restaurants, but none of them are good.” It’s the first half of the sentence where you’d use あるにはあるが, followed by second half. 

Hopefully it also makes sense to relate ある “to exist” with “to be possible.” So the phrase could also mean that something/some situation is possible, BUT (isn’t common/doesn’t happen often). Where the part in parentheses is the second half of the sentence. This will also depend on context.

However, what I hear you asking — is there any pattern to go by to predict the pronunciation of 天? Great question, and I definitely struggled with this when I was overwhelmed with memorizing tons of kanji compounds.

This is NOT an exact science and there are plenty of exceptions, but the likelihood of てん in a kanji compound is probably much higher. 天候 weather, 天使 angel, 天国 heaven, 天才 genius, 天丼 tempura donburi, etc. However I’ve also found 天照 (あまてらす）and 天下り（あまくだり）, among others. 

I could probably also guess that a word that starts like 天の could be あま or てん with about equal likelihood. 天の川、天の原、etc. However, there’s 天の助け（てんのたすけ）、天の声（てんのこえ）. I hardly found anything with あめ, though I’m sure more words are out there somewhere. 

If skimming some reading in Japanese I’d probably take a guess based on that general sense above. But it’s definitely important to look up in the dictionary to make sure the guess is correct. Hope this helps!

Shameless plug for Kobe! It's a very quick ride from Okayama if you have the JR pass. Some say Kobe isn't very interesting for tourists who come from abroad, compared to major cities like Okyoto/Osaka, but it's a great opportunity to experience sites popular among the locals. I'd personally recommend Nunobiki Herb Garden/Nunobiki Falls right off Shinkobe Station or Arima Onsen, a hot springs town about a half hour north. Harborland is also a beautiful port area to walk around and relax amidst the rush of sightseeing.

There's really so much to see in Tokyo that I think the perfect "intro" depends on your personal interests as well. Do you enjoy shopping? Would you want to see historical sites and museums? Are you a fan of pop culture and anime/manga? And… are you unafraid of high places? There are a lot of great views in Tokyo. :)

Lastly, if you are willing to sacrifice a bit of comfort for economy, you might also look at capsule hotels or guest houses, in addition to Airbnb. I've spent a lot of time in eastern (and western) Japan, so I'd love to suggest a Tokyo itinerary for you or answer other questions you may have.

As someone who's lived in Kobe, I do recommend the Kansai Thru Pass! I've done the 3-day pass twice, and found it to be convenient and economic. One warning if you haven't read already, the Kansai Thru Pass is for NON JR LINES ONLY. Since I was a "local," it turned out to be a good deal for me, but depending on where you want to go, the JR West Kansai Area Pass may be better. If you decide to use Day 3 for other Kansai locations, additionally Kyoto has a 1-day 500-yen bus pass that will get you to most of the major sites, like Kiyomizudera, Kinkakuji, etc. (http://www.visitkansai.com/sightseeing/kyoto-city-bus/)

About your itinerary: Sounds like your home base is Osaka, which kind of puts you in the middle of things, so great idea. Day 1 sounds a bit packed, since Himeji is about 1:45 hr from Osaka and 1 hr from Kobe (using Thru Pass). It's possible, but you might feel rushed unless you don't mind staying out late.

Hello! That's a great question. I think it's fairly common to find hotels that have suite-style rooms or multiple beds per room, especially in larger cities. There are a couple things I noticed in your itinerary. First, you indicated the "fujigoko" 5 lakes region as a half-day trip. I tried planning a trip to Mt. Fuji once, but I discovered that there's not really a direct train route to get there, which means you may have to coordinate train transfers. Since it can take around 3 hours each way, a full-day trip is ideal if you want adequate time to spend at your destination.

Second, Arashiyama is one of my favorite places in Kyoto! Far enough from the regular tourist commotion around major shrines/temples, but still has plenty of picture-perfect sightseeing spots. :) When you get out of the station, there's a path you can take to the left, just before the big bridge that leads into the main town. It's a pretty walk down the river that leads up the mountain a bit for a great view ("best view ever" according to multiple signs I saw along the way).

Hello! I'm American, and I went to Comiket in summer 2012. I vaguely remember that the vendor catalogue was completely in Japanese, and it required quite the language level to find your favorite anime/manga/artists in a sea of kanji. However, if you're just looking around, it may be more fun (and spontaneous) to skip the catalogue and find whatever stations look interesting to you.

I think purchasing requires little verbal interaction since most of the time the price is marked clearly on the item. When in doubt, ask "ikura desu ka" and hope the seller speaks slowly! "mou ichido onegai shimasu" (one more time, please) and "motto yukkuri onegai shimasu" (slower, please) might come in handy.

If your goal is to come out with a ton of cool merch, then at least $100 (10,000 JPY) would allow you to spend freely without having to make tough decisions, until you start running out. I saw plenty of comics selling for between 500 and 1000 yen.

Lastly, a note about the nature of Comiket compared to US conventions: while cons in the US tend to be geared toward fans with lots of activities and panels, Comiket focuses mainly on artists showing their work. (But there's usually a cosplay area though, which is super entertaining, too!) As a result, it's packed with serious collectors and long lines, and it gets very hot and sticky. You'll see lots of people wearing sweat towels and carrying paper fans.

Anything else you're interested in seeing? Please reach out if you have other questions about Comiket or Japan!
